title: Ekachakri Nagaram and Bakasura
body:
Ekachakri Nagaram and Bakasura

कृतज्ञता परो धर्मः कृतज्ञता परं तपः।
यः कृतज्ञो भवेल्लोके स एव पुरुषोत्तमः॥

"Gratitude is the highest righteousness, and gratitude is the supreme austerity. One who is truly grateful in this world is indeed a jewel among human beings."

Disguised as simple mendicant Brahmanas, the Pandavas settled in the peaceful town of Ekachakra, finding shelter in the house of a poor Brahmana landlord. Each day, the brothers went out to beg for alms, returning to share their collections with their mother. One afternoon, while Bhima remained behind with Kunti, loud, agonising lamentations arose from the inner chambers of their host. Kunti entered to find the family in utter despair. The father was weeping: 'I cannot send you, my beloved wife, to the monster; nor can I sacrifice my daughter or my little baby boy.' The wife insisted on going, followed by the daughter's brave plea: 'I am but a single soul; let me be the boat to carry you across this river of calamity.' Even the baby boy, brandishing a stick of firewood, lisped: 'I shall kill the monster with this!'
Kunti learnt that the town was terrorised by a cannibalistic demon named Bakasura. By an ancient agreement to prevent indiscriminate slaughter, each household was required to send a cartload of food, two buffaloes, and a human being to the demon's cave each week; the demon would consume the entire offering, including the human carrier. It was now the Brahmana host's turn. Kunti immediately declared: 'Do not weep. I have five sons. One of them shall carry this food to the demon and save your family.' Yudhishthira, upon returning, was filled with panic: 'Mother, is this not rash? It is upon Bhima's strength that we sleep without care, and hope to regain our kingdom. Why risk his life?'
Kunti's reply was firm and anchored in the highest principles of Visishtadvaita ethics: 'Dear son, we have lived happily in the house of this Brahmana. Gratitude (Kritagnata) is man's highest virtue; to repay the benefits we have enjoyed by doing good in return is our sacred duty. I know Bhima's strength; he who carried us from the flames of Varanavata will surely crush this demon.' Bhima went to the cave, calmly ate the food before the demon's eyes, and in the titanic combat that followed, tore the demon apart, freeing the town from terror. This chapter highlights the inseparable integration (Aprathaksiddhi) of all souls. The suffering of our host must be felt as our own suffering; active moral reciprocity is the only true practical worship of Sriman Narayana.
